extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and copyeditors (academic and book publishing)
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from a traditional manual of style giving prescriptive rules for punctuation marks (periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, hyphens, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, apostrophes, etc.), with examples and exceptions for use in academic/book publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for punctuation style
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Keep punctuation in same font as preceding character; illustrated by quotation examples and references to numbered rules. (Original wording: 'All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word, letter, or character immediately preceding them.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Period: end of sentence, abbreviations, placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence; put a period after most abbreviations, with specified exceptions; do not use a period after certain symbols or roman numerals; placement inside quotation marks and parentheses depends on syntactic independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes: (122) Period = end of complete sentence. (123) Put a period after all abbreviations except when omission is indicated by an apostrophe; treat metric symbols as abbreviations but not chemical symbols, nor 'per cent' nor book formats. (Note) Exceptions for measure symbols in certain journals. (124) Use no period after Roman numerals even if ordinal. (125) Omit period after running-heads, centered headlines, side-heads set in separate lines, cut-in heads, box-heads in tables, superscriptions/legends not forming a complete sentence, date lines at top of communications, and after signatures. (126) Place period inside quotation marks; inside parentheses only when the enclosed matter is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point: use and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the exclamation point to mark an outcry, emphatic or ironical utterance; place it inside quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quotation or parenthetical matter, otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for emphatic quotations and dialogue (127). Cross-reference to placement rule (128). (Original wording: 'The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance... The exclamation point is placed inside the quotation marks or parentheses when part of the quotation or parenthetical matter; otherwise outside.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point (question mark): use and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the interrogation point to mark a query or express doubt; do not use it after indirect questions; place it inside quotation marks or parentheses only when it is part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: direct question in quotes, marking doubtful names with parentheses; indirect question example ('He asked whether he was ill.') that should not take a question mark. (Original wording summarized from 129-130.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon: function and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A colon marks a discontinuity greater than a semicolon and less than a period; commonly used to (i) emphasize a close connection between two complete clauses, (ii) separate a complete clause from an illustrative/amplifying clause, (iii) introduce formal statements, extracts, speeches in dialogue, etc.; placement outside quotation marks unless part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes when to use a comma instead (before a clause quoted mid-sentence), use as substitute for 'namely/as follows/for instance', put a colon after salutatory phrases in letters and introductory remarks to an audience, use centered colon in Scripture/time and between place and publisher in references, and place colon outside quotation marks unless part of quotation. Examples and counterexamples given (131-136).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon: function and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a semicolon to mark a division of a sentence more independent than a comma; use semicolons in complex enumerations and between closely connected clauses; place semicolon outside quotation marks or parentheses unless part of the quoted or parenthetical matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show semicolons joining clauses that could be separate sentences, use in enumerations where links are long or contain internal punctuation (138), scripture passage separation involving chapters (139), and placement rule (140).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma: general function and principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A comma indicates the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, contributing to clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manual provides many numbered subrules (141 onward). Highlights: use comma to separate proper nouns belonging to different individuals/places (142); use comma before conjunctions 'and/or/nor' in a series of three or more (serial/Oxford comma) except in brief, close-knit phrases (143); ordinarily put a comma before and after clauses introduced by conjunctions like 'and', 'but', 'if', 'while', etc., especially if the subject changes (144); omit comma where the connection is logically close; use comma after introductory conjunctive/adverbial words ('now','then','however','moreover', etc.) when they begin a sentence or clause that introduces inference or explanation, and set them off with commas when wedged into the middle of a sentence; exceptions noted when the terms are closely connected and don't require a pause (145). Also: omit comma before 'rather' in specified expressions (146); rules for commas with adjectives (147), participial clauses (148), commas before 'not' introducing antithetical clauses (149); use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional clauses (150); separate identical/closely similar words with a comma (151); use commas in adjectival phrases with complementary/antithetical adjectives (152); separate coordinate clauses ending in a word governing another clause (153); use commas to separate two numbers and to indicate omitted words (154-155); put a comma before brief direct quotations (156); use comma with 'of' for residence/position (157); various exceptions for references, thousands separators, month/year separation, signatures and address lines, and comma placement relative to quotation marks and parentheses (158-162). Many examples and journal-specific notes accompany these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe: contractions and possessive formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe to mark omitted letters/figures in contractions and numbers; form possessive case of nouns (common and proper) with an apostrophe or apostrophe+s depending on rules and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include contractions (ne'er, don't), class of '96; possessives: a man's word, horses' tails, Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's forais, Themistocles' era, and special cases like appearance' sake (163-164). Also addresses plural of numerals and rare coinages formed using apostrophe and s (165) with examples ('in the 1900's', 'the Y.M.C.A.'s').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks: placement (cross-reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks are treated elsewhere (see 'Quotations' section); placement rules for periods and commas given (they are placed inside quotation marks), with other punctuation placed depending on grammatical relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This chunk cross-references sections 74-91 for quotations; also reiterates that commas and periods go inside quotation marks (see 126, 162) and other marks (colons, semicolons) generally outside unless part of the quoted matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dashes (em/en): uses and punctuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use dashes to denote sudden breaks, abrupt changes, long pauses, or epigrammatic turns; use dashes for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent; use a dash to introduce clauses of emphasis or explanation and where 'namely' is implied; precede summarizing clauses with a dash; use a dash after a run-in or side-head; use dash conventions for ranges and references in citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: interruptive phrases, repeated words for emphasis, parenthetical clauses that deserve stronger separation than commas (166-170). Use dashes for run-in side-heads and to connect references after quotations in footnotes (174). Avoid combining dashes with other punctuation points except periods (175). Guidance includes en dash vs em dash for date and page ranges: May–July (en dash), May 1, 1905 — November 1, 1906 (em dash); pp. 3-7 (en dash) and rules for repeating hundreds in ranges and journal exceptions (173).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses: enumeration and restrictive use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parentheses to enclose figures/letters used to mark divisions in enumerations run into text; use single parentheses with lower-case italic letters for paragraphed divisions; do not ordinarily use parentheses for parenthetical clauses except when necessary to avoid confusion or when the content is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides example enumerations and a conventional schema for heads and subheads (176). Advises preferring dashes for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent, and using parentheses only when confusion would arise or content is irrelevant (177).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets: uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Use brackets to enclose explanations/notes, indicate interpolations in quotations, rectify mistakes, supply omissions, and for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: editorial notes [This was written before...—Editor], clarifying bracketed phrases in quotations, correcting names with bracketed letters, supply omissions in bibliographic citations, and using brackets for nested parentheses (178-179). Also instructs bracketed continuation lines like '[Continued from p. 320]' (179).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses: indicating omissions and lacunae
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate omission from a quotation of nonessential words and illegible or mutilated words; use four periods (with spacing) for an ellipsis at beginning/middle/end of sentence (except French uses three); if a preceding line ends in a point, do not include it in the four; for omitted whole paragraphs or lines in poetry, insert a full line of periods spaced appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat an ellipsis as part of the citation and enclose it in quotation marks (181). Examples show use in prose and poetry and note variation for narrow measures and languages (180-181).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphens: general hyphenation principles
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is used at line breaks to carry a syllable to the next line and between many compound words; hyphenate compound adjectives preceding a noun, compounds where one component contains multiple words use an en dash, do not hyphenate adverb+adjective when adverb ends in -ly, and follow many specific hyphenation rules for various compound types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive guidance (182 onward). Key points and examples: hyphenate adjectives formed from multiple words before a noun (well-known author, first-class investment); use en dash when a component contains more than one word (New York–Chicago freight traffic); avoid hyphen with adverbs ending in -ly and in certain post-nominal adjective positions. Specific rules for nouns formed by combining two nouns in objective relation (mind-reader, story-teller) with exceptions (lawgiver, taxpayer). Hyphenate present-participle + noun formations (boarding-house), and follow rules for compounds with book/house/mill/room/shop/work according to syllable count (handbook vs pocket-book; boathouse vs engine-house). Occupation compounds usually hyphenated (harness-maker); compounds of 'store', 'fellow', kin words, 'great-' (great-grandfather), 'life', 'world', 'skin', 'master', 'god' compounds, 'half', 'quarter' with hyphen, rules for prefixes like semi-, demi-, bi-, tri- (usually no hyphen except long/unusual cases), compounds beginning with 'self-' (self-evident), combinations with 'fold' (twofold vs fifteen fold), adjectives formed with suffixation 'like' (childlike vs eel-like), titles parts (vice-, ex-, elect-, general-), 'by-' compounds (by-product, by-laws), and rules for prefixes 'co-', 'pre-', 're-' when followed by same vowel or w/y (co-operation, re-enter) with many exceptions and journal variants noted (203-204). Also lists words that omit hyphen (today, tomorrow, tonight, viewpoint, standpoint) and notes that negative particles 'im-', 'in-', 'a-' do not usually require a hyphen (204-205). Many illustrative examples and exceptions are provided throughout the hyphenation section.
